And the Tatars accepted his favour concerning this.
And he said again: "An amir, one of ours,
namely the son of Ghatir (Ibn Qatir),
wishes to take the youth Ghiyath al-Din, the lord of the land of the Romans, and to flee to Egypt.
Therefore give me an army,
that I may go and seize him in haste."
And when Qungqurtai, the younger brother of the King of Kings, went with him,
they found the son of Khatir and the youth Sultan in the plain of Albistan, as they were wishing to flee to Syria.
And when he killed the son of Ghatir,
he delivered the Sultan to the Parwana,
and he seated him again upon the throne of his kingdom.
And thus that Parwana became very great in the eyes of the Tatars,
and was greatly beloved by them,
because of the sincerity of the love that he showed them.
At this time, when A'lam al-Din Jacob, the great merchant, a Christian man
from Barqawta, a village in the territory of Erbil,
was returning from the service of Kublai, the Great Khan,
he died on the way in the land of Khurasan.
Now Ashmut, the envoy who had been appointed with him—
who was also a great and honourable man, of the race of the Uighurs,
and was walking in the way of monkhood—
took his sons and brought them into the service of the King of Kings, Abaqa.
And he received them well,
and appointed Mas'ud, the eldest son, over Mosul and Erbil,
and that aforesaid Ashmut became his governor.
And in this same year in which Mas'ud was made to reign,
which is the year 1587 {OCR?}
[of the Greeks],
another son of Sheikh Adi also fled from the territory of Mosul to Egypt,
and he also took with him the Mongol woman whom he had taken from the Tatars.
And in the year 1588
[of the Greeks] that Bunduqdar, the lord of Egypt, resolved in his mind
to enter the land of the Romans in person.
For Baysar the elder, with other amirs from the land of the Romans
who had fled to him,
incited him to this.
Now King Leon of Cilicia, when he perceived this,
sent and informed the commanders of the Tatar armies to be on their guard,
because the Egyptian was preparing to conquer them.
The Parwana, however, either because of his hatred for the king of the Armenians,
or because his heart was not upright toward the Tatars,
showed him to be a liar before the chiefs of the Tatars.
